picks.title: Winning Over Translation
picks.take: Honigsfeld, Dove and McDermott Goldman argue that leaning on translation alone can stall a newcomer's English, content learning and social growth, and they are not against translation. They offer dos and don'ts: translate on purpose, check AI output with a fluent speaker, keep the English original alongside, and never use students or siblings for sensitive content.
picks.try: Hand a newcomer the English text next to the translation and ask for one sentence back in English before you accept the translated notes.

picks.title: An Important Point About “Making Student Learning Visible To Students Themselves” & A Bunch Of Ways To Do Just That
picks.take: Ferlazzo picks up John Warner's point that students who can see their own growth have less reason to reach for AI shortcuts. His own moves: a vocabulary checklist returned at unit end, rewriting an August essay for the final, and recorded repeated readings. He adds a dozen low-prep options, from confidence ratings to fluency graphs.
picks.try: Give students the unit vocabulary list on day one, have them mark what they know, and return the same sheet on the last day to mark again.

picks.title: The Best Fun Videos For English Language Learners In 2026 – Part Two
picks.take: A fresh batch of short, funny clips Ferlazzo uses with ELLs for speaking, listening and writing, mostly animal videos, a Super Bowl ad and a Colbert song remake with a lyrics video. One clip looks AI-made, which he suggests turning into a class discussion. Useful for the week before Thanksgiving break when attention is thin.
picks.try: Play one 30-second clip twice with no sound, have pairs narrate the sequence orally, then write it in three sentences using first, then, finally.
